name: data-transfer-object
intent: Bundle the fields a boundary crossing needs into one data-only, serializable object so a single coarse-grained call carries the whole payload while the domain model and the wire representation stay independent.
problem: Calls across a remote or layer boundary cost far more than the work they do. Fetching a payload field by field means many round trips, and handing the domain object graph to a serializer means lazy-loading faults, cycles, leaked internal structure and a wire shape nobody designed. The recurring trigger: carry a whole payload over the boundary in one serializable object.
context: Boundary-crossing calls where per-call cost dominates: remote interfaces and Remote Facades, service-to-service APIs, message payloads on a bus, and in-process layer boundaries where the domain model must not leak into presentation or integration code. It applies when the consumer needs a specific, curated set of fields rather than the domain object, and when the wire shape must evolve on its own schedule (versioning, several consuming languages, generated schemas).
benefits: One coarse-grained call replaces a chatty sequence of fine-grained ones, so round trips and their latency drop sharply - the reason the pattern exists.
The wire shape becomes an explicit, named contract: which fields cross, under which names and types, is a deliberate allow-list instead of whatever the domain object graph happens to expose.
Serialization is encapsulated in the carrier (Fowler's 2013 note): encoding and format concerns stay out of domain and application code, and switching format is a local change.
The domain model stays private and free to evolve: renames, added internals and new invariants do not automatically become breaking API changes.
Boundary logic becomes testable in isolation: an assembler plus DTO is a pure mapping that can be exercised without a network, database or container.
Lazy-loading and cycle surprises at serialization time disappear: the payload is flat, materialised and complete before it reaches the serializer.
Data exposure is controlled per boundary: sensitive fields (password hashes, internal IDs, audit columns) are excluded by construction rather than convention.
Separate request and response DTOs allow independent evolution: input validation constraints and output shaping change for different reasons.
Generated schema-first DTOs (protobuf, OpenAPI, Avro) provide cross-language type safety at the wire level without hand-written parallel type hierarchies.
DTOs prevent over-posting attacks: mutable request DTOs with explicit allow-listed fields block clients from setting server-controlled or internal fields.
Immutability (especially with language records/data classes) makes DTOs safe for concurrent and distributed contexts where payloads must not change after construction.
tradeoffs: Field duplication: the DTO mirrors domain fields, so a new domain field means touching domain, DTO, assembler and mapping tests - the pattern's best-known cost.
Assembler code and its bugs: mapping is mechanical, easy to get subtly wrong (missing field, wrong default, unchecked coercion) and drifts quietly unless it is kept under test.
Coarse payloads over-fetch: a consumer that needs one field pays for the whole object, and a careless DTO ships more data - including sensitive data - than the call requires.
Temptation to promote the DTO to domain model: once the carrier is convenient, invariants migrate into it and the domain becomes anemic, while mutable DTOs used as shared state destroy encapsulation.
Extra allocation and copying per crossing (a second object per entity, deep copies, serialization buffers), which is measurable for high-frequency in-process calls where no real boundary exists.
Versioning debt: a published wire shape can only be evolved additively; renames and removals become contract changes with compatibility rules (tag numbers, optional fields, deprecation windows).
Bi-directional entity relationships mapped naively cause infinite recursion at serialization time unless one side is explicitly ignored.
Reflection-based mappers (e.g., ModelMapper) silently ignore unmapped fields, masking contract drift until production.
Mapping outside a transaction boundary triggers LazyInitializationException for ORM-managed associations fetched lazily.

Fetching entities then mapping to DTOs loses the performance benefit of direct DTO projections: JPA's persistence context management, dirty checking, and entity caching add overhead for read-only payloads (Thorben Janssen, thorben-janssen.com).

participants.responsibility: A serializable, data-only container holding exactly the fields that cross the boundary (plus transport metadata); it carries no domain behaviour and knows nothing about persistence. Often modelled as an immutable type (Java record, Kotlin data class, C# record, Python frozen dataclass, TypeScript interface).

The single place that translates domain objects into DTOs and back; it is the only component that knows both shapes and keeps the mapping under test. Can be hand-written, generated by MapStruct (compile-time, type-safe), or a combination.
The remote interface or layer entry point that accepts and returns DTOs (Remote Facade, API controller, message handler); it orchestrates domain work and delegates mapping to the assembler.
Holds business state and behaviour - identity, invariants, rules; it never crosses the boundary itself.
Encodes the DTO into the wire format (JSON, protobuf, XML, Avro, ...) and back; it works from the DTO's public shape only and must never need to traverse the domain.

use_cases: Web/REST API responses and request bodies: project entities into response DTOs so the API shape is curated, lazy-loading proxies never leak and internal refactors do not break clients.
Remote Facade methods: batch many fine-grained getters and setters into one serializable parameter and return payload (the pattern's original PoEAA setting).
Service-to-service messages: a schema-first payload (protobuf, JSON, Avro) generated from an IDL and consumed by services written in different languages.
Layer boundaries inside one process: hand the presentation or integration layer a DTO instead of a domain entity when the domain must stay independent (hexagonal/onion ports).
Bulk transfer and reporting: ship a bounded set of rows (a Record Set) for export, sync or an admin screen without exposing query or ORM internals.
Anti-corruption boundaries: DTOs at the edge of a legacy or third-party system, keeping that system's shape out of the core model.
CQRS read models: query-side projections that return flat, denormalised DTOs optimised for the specific read pattern rather than the domain aggregate.
Event-driven messaging contracts: DTOs as typed message payloads on Kafka, RabbitMQ or SNS/SQS, where the schema must be versioned and independently evolved from producers and consumers.

Protobuf-first hybrid REST+gRPC: generate Java DTOs from .proto files and use ProtobufJsonFormatHttpMessageConverter in Spring to serve REST/JSON directly from generated protobuf objects, eliminating hand-written parallel DTOs.
Database read projections: Spring Data JPA projection interfaces or constructor-based DTO projections where the repository query selects only the needed columns and maps directly to the DTO.
BFF (Backend for Frontend) API composition: aggregate data from multiple microservices into a single DTO shaped for a specific frontend client (mobile, web, third-party).
Saga choreography messages: each saga step exchanges typed command/event DTOs that carry just enough state for the next step to act, without exposing the full aggregate.
GraphQL resolver response shaping: map domain objects to a DTO that matches the exact selection set the client requested, avoiding over-fetching in a field-level resolution context.

Laravel API Resources: JsonResource subclasses with an explicit toArray transformation layer between Eloquent models and JSON responses, controlling which attributes and relationships are visible per user or endpoint.
ASP.NET Core minimal APIs: Microsoft's official tutorial swaps EF Core entities for a TodoItemDTO at every endpoint, blocking over-posting and keeping internal fields (Secret) off the wire.

Protobuf-generated message classes as the wire DTO: protobuf.dev tag/wire-type encoding lets consumers compiled against older .proto definitions skip unknown fields, so the payload evolves without hand-written carrier types.
avoid_when: In-process calls on the same object graph where passing the domain object is cheap and safe - the mapping buys nothing; use a Parameter Object when the argument list is long.
The framework already projects at the boundary (ORM read models, serializer field filtering, GraphQL selection, generated gRPC types you own) - do not hand-write assembly on top of it.
The domain is already a plain immutable data structure with no behaviour (functional core, records all the way down) - a parallel DTO only duplicates the shape.
The call carries one or two values: a plain argument or a small tuple is clearer than a carrier type.
The client needs domain behaviour, not data: shipping DTOs to a rich client only relocates the domain and yields an anemic model on both sides.
The DTO mechanically mirrors every entity field one-to-one with no curation - no boundary protection is gained, only ceremony.

Direct entity-to-DTO mapping for read-only queries: fetching a managed JPA entity then mapping it discards the performance benefit of unmanaged DTO projections; prefer JPQL constructor expressions or Tuple Transformers that instantiate DTOs directly from the result set (Thorben Janssen).
anti_patterns: DTO as domain model: business rules, invariant validation and persistence annotations migrate into the DTO, leaving an anemic domain with duplicated rules.
"Just serialize the entity": JSON-encoding ORM entities directly - leaks internal columns, triggers lazy loads or serialization cycles and publishes every newly added field.
DTO explosion: a separate near-identical DTO per screen, endpoint or call site, with shapes drifting apart and no single contract to version.
Mutable DTOs used as shared state: public setters as a programming model, so any holder can rewrite the payload in transit and invariants become unenforceable.
Chatty DTOs: carriers holding a single field, or one DTO per field access, keeping the boundary as chatty as before with extra ceremony.
Mapping without tests: reflection or annotation mappers plus silent field-name mismatches, so the payload loses fields nobody notices until production.
Bidirectional entity serialization loops: exposing both sides of a one-to-many relationship in DTOs without @JsonIgnore causes infinite recursion at runtime.
One DTO reused for create, read, update and delete: conflating mutable input, immutable output and authorisation fields makes the contract incoherent and the boundary leaky.

Fetching entities then mapping to DTOs for read-only operations: JPA entity management overhead (persistence context, dirty checking, proxy initialization) is paid for no benefit when the DTO is the final consumer.
God DTO: a single DTO with all optional fields for every use case makes validation incoherent and accidentally exposes server-controlled fields to clients.
Local DTO abuse: applying the pattern inside a single process boundary where a plain argument or domain object would be cleaner and faster (Fowler's LocalDTO bliki).
design_principles: Single responsibility: the DTO carries data, the assembler maps, the domain owns behaviour.
Information hiding: the domain model is not published; the wire contract is an explicit allow-list.
Separation of concerns: transport representation and domain representation change for different reasons and must not be coupled.
Dependency direction: the domain must not depend on transport, serialization or presentation concerns; DTOs and assemblers depend on the domain, never the reverse.
Make boundaries explicit: a named payload type makes the crossing visible and reviewable, unlike an implicit object-graph walk.
Version contracts deliberately: the wire shape is an interface, and interfaces need compatibility rules.
Immutability by default: immutable DTOs are safer in concurrent and distributed contexts; mutability is the exception justified by framework requirements.
Validation at the boundary, invariants in the domain: DTO-level validation (nullability, format, range) is a contract concern; domain invariants are a business concern enforced inside the boundary.
Shape the DTO for the consumer, not the domain: DTO fields should reflect what the caller needs, not how the data is stored internally.
One assembler per boundary, both directions tested: keep the mapping logic co-located and exercise round-trip (domain→DTO→domain) in unit tests.
Prefer direct DTO projections for reads: construct DTOs from query result sets rather than materializing entities then mapping, to avoid ORM management overhead on read-only paths.
best_practices: Keep DTOs immutable where the language allows (records, final fields, frozen, readonly) so a payload cannot be rewritten between production and consumption.
Keep one assembler per boundary with both directions in the same module and unit-test the round trip (domain -> DTO -> domain), including defaults and absent fields.
Curate fields as an allow-list: never derive the DTO blindly from the entity and never ship credentials, internal identifiers or audit columns.
Model absence explicitly (optional/nullable/oneof/default) instead of relying on zero values, and fix the field-naming strategy once for the whole API.
Version additively: add optional fields, never reuse or renumber protobuf tags, and keep a deprecation window for removals.
Prefer schema-first generation (protobuf, OpenAPI, Avro) when several services or languages consume the same payload; hand-written parallel DTOs drift.
Keep payloads flat: avoid cyclic graphs, embed only what the consumer needs, and paginate genuinely large results.
Separate request DTOs from response DTOs: create, update, summary, detail and event payloads have different fields, nullability and validation rules and should not be shared.
Validate at the boundary, not the domain: apply @NotNull, @Email, @Size (or equivalent) on request DTOs; enforce domain invariants in the domain layer only.

Use compile-time mappers (e.g., MapStruct) over reflection-based ones (e.g., ModelMapper) in production: MapStruct generates plain method calls at compile time with full type safety; ModelMapper uses reflection and silently ignores unmapped fields.
Keep DTOs in the boundary or adapter layer, not in the domain package: the domain must not import serialization annotations or transport metadata types.
Handle lazy loading before mapping: fetch all required associations eagerly (JOIN FETCH, EntityGraph) or map inside the same transaction that loads the entity.
Configure Jackson to omit null fields globally (@JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL)) or per-DTO; explicitly model nullable vs absent rather than relying on zero-values.
Use @JsonIgnore or dedicated read-only DTO projections for bidirectional entity relationships to prevent infinite recursion during serialization.
For protobuf-first hybrid REST+gRPC: generate the DTO once from .proto and use ProtobufJsonFormatHttpMessageConverter to serve REST/JSON directly, eliminating parallel hand-written DTOs.

Document and enforce unknown-field policies: servers must tolerate unknown response fields (additive evolution); consider rejecting unknown request fields on write operations to catch client typos early.

For read-only queries, prefer direct DTO projections (JPQL constructor expressions, TupleTransformer, Hibernate's @SqlResultSetMapping) over entity-fetch-then-map; this skips JPA's persistence context management overhead entirely.

Use distinct DTOs per BFF (Backend for Frontend) client: mobile, web, and third-party consumers often need different field subsets and shapes; aggregate into a per-client DTO rather than one oversized contract.
Name DTOs by their purpose, not the entity: OrderCreateRequest, OrderSummaryResponse, OrderEventPayload — not just OrderDto — so the contract boundary is self-documenting.

Prefer composition over deep nesting in DTOs: a flat DTO with foreign keys or embedded value objects is easier for consumers to parse than a multi-level object graph that may cause N+1 query explosions.

Treat DTOs as the only entry point for external data: never let raw external payloads (incoming webhooks, file imports, third-party API responses) deserialize directly into domain objects; always deserialize into a DTO first, then map.
